stories.topic: The Economist Who Puked on a Forest
stories.summary: On a two-hour tandem paragliding ride in the mountains near Beer, the air turned rocky at the highest point. The pilot, behind him, gently instructed Ajay how to stick his head out and puke on the forest below. Amit deadpans: are you the first economist to puke on a forest?
stories.insight: A small, self-deprecating opener that signals the show's register: serious ideas delivered without self-importance. The capacity to laugh at one's own undignified moments is part of what keeps the conversation honest.

stories.topic: The Free Rental Market of 1942 Bombay
stories.summary: Around 1976, at the family dinner table, Ajay's father told the four kids that when he first came to Bombay in 1942 (during the Quit India Movement), you could just walk around the streets and within fifteen minutes rent a flat. The 1970s kids were wide-eyed: in their lifetime, renting in Bombay was nearly impossible because of rent control and the pugadi system. The contrast was unbelievable to them.
stories.insight: Rent control's worst harm is invisible to anyone born after it: a generation grows up assuming the dysfunction is a law of nature. The story is a vivid reminder that markets we now consider broken were once frictionless, and that policy choices wrote the brokenness in.

stories.topic: The Bengali Bureaucrat and the Jute Industry
stories.summary: Amit once asked a senior West Bengal bureaucrat what the funda with jute was. The reply: jute is our indigenous industry, the government has to keep it alive, so subsidies, price controls, land grants, this and that. Amit pushed back: why does the government have any role to play here? If there's demand for jute, let supply meet it. The bureaucrat refused to engage further. (Forty-five milliseconds later, Ajay reveals that jute today has actually thrived without the state, riding technological forces all by itself.)
stories.insight: The technocratic instinct is to 'save' an industry; the libertarian instinct is to ask whether it needs saving at all. The punchline that jute prospered on its own is a perfect Hazlitt-style demonstration: the unseen alternative was the industry succeeding without state coddling.

stories.topic: Lant Pritchett's Origin Story With This Book
stories.summary: On The Seen and the Unseen, Lant Pritchett told Amit that Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson was the book that turned him onto economics. More recently, one of Ajay's mentees (a 'mini Ajay') told Amit the same book was her entry into the subject. Across generations and continents, the same little 1946 primer keeps doing the work.
stories.insight: Some books punch above their weight not because they say new things but because they crystallise old truths so cleanly that they become 'light bulbs' in young minds. The longevity of Hazlitt's book is itself a testimony to the durability of fundamental economic principles.

stories.topic: The Friend Who Didn't Know Libertarians Cared
stories.summary: Years ago, an ardent leftist friend said to Amit, 'I didn't realise you cared so much. I thought you're a libertarian, you don't give a shit.' The remark startled Amit because it captured a widespread misunderstanding: that compassion is the proprietary preserve of one political side, and the other side must therefore lack it.
stories.insight: The defining sin of much of the left, per Daniel Hannan, is not its policies but its certainty that compassion is unique to it. The libertarian's critique of price controls or welfare schemes is itself an act of compassion that asks: do these actually help the people they claim to?

stories.topic: From Frozen Chicken to Electric Vehicles at JNPT
stories.summary: Ajay's parable: there are two ways to make an electric vehicle. One is the Mahindra factory at Igatpuri, where thousands of workers assemble lithium-ion batteries and motors. The other is on the poultry farms of Maharashtra: you make containers of frozen chicken, send them out from JNPT (Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust), and on the high seas, magically, they turn into electric vehicles arriving at JNPT. That magical conversion is a technology called trade.
stories.insight: Trade is a technology, no different from a steam engine or a CPU. Treating tariffs as an industrial policy that favours the Igatpuri-EV-maker over the JNPT-EV-maker reveals the absurdity of protectionism: you are picking a winner among two equally valid production methods.

stories.topic: The Tatsuo Horio Painting Made in Excel
stories.summary: Ajay produced a painting by Japanese artist Tatsuo Horio and challenged Amit to identify the medium. The answer: Microsoft Excel. The artist had used the same spreadsheet tool whose adoption Ajay had just lamented as still incomplete in Indian businesses, decades after its arrival.
stories.insight: Arthur C. Clarke's line that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic applies here: a tool we think we know (Excel) becomes a paintbrush in the right hands. The story doubles as a counter-Luddite parable — even when adoption is slow, the long tail of unexpected uses keeps surprising us.

recommendations.item: Economics in One Lesson
recommendations.creator: Henry Hazlitt
recommendations.context: The 1946 primer that is the spine of this entire episode.
recommendations.reason: Hazlitt's book remains the cleanest articulation of two ideas: trace the longer-run consequences of any policy, and trace its consequences for all groups, not just the one it visibly helps. The fallacies he wrote against in 1946 are alive in 2025; that is precisely why the book endures and why both Lant Pritchett and a young 'mini Ajay' point to it as their entry into economics.

recommendations.item: Basic Economics
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: The other foundational primer Amit returns to repeatedly.
recommendations.reason: Alongside Hazlitt, Sowell's Basic Economics is one of the few works Amit names when asked for a single fundamental book on economics.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on Indian public policy.
recommendations.reason: An important book for anyone wanting to understand both public policy and its application to India — two books' worth of primer in one volume.

recommendations.item: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Episode 45)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on recurring economic fallacies.
recommendations.reason: The same fallacies Hazlitt diagnosed in 1946 are catalogued and dissected here in modern Indian context.

recommendations.item: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on luxury beliefs.
recommendations.reason: Many modern fashionable opinions are 'luxury beliefs' — held to signal status — that ride on the very fallacies Hazlitt warns against.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Price System (Episode 66)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on the dangers of price controls.
recommendations.reason: Sets up the case that price controls invariably produce shortages — context for Hazlitt's chapters on price control, rent control and the minimum wage.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive with Lant Pritchett.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Pritchett describes how Hazlitt's book turned him onto economics, and where he argues that growth correlates around 99% with human welfare indicators.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on four foundational economics papers.
recommendations.reason: Includes a discussion of Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' — the essay that gave Amit the lightbulb moment about how prices work.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's classic 1945 paper.
recommendations.reason: The essay that flipped Amit's intuition on the price system — once you understand how decentralised price information aggregates dispersed knowledge, you cannot un-see the folly of central price-fixing.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen and the Unseen episode with Matt Ridley.
recommendations.reason: Where Ridley walks Amit through how spontaneous order runs through everything from languages to prices — a companion 'lightbulb' to Hayek.

recommendations.item: The Evolution of Everything
recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Ridley's book on bottom-up explanations of complex systems.
recommendations.reason: The book that made Amit see spontaneous order as the unifying frame across biology, language, markets and society.

recommendations.item: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
recommendations.creator: Frederic Bastiat
recommendations.context: Bastiat's mid-19th-century essay containing the parable of the broken window.
recommendations.reason: The essay that inspired both Hazlitt's book and Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen. The broken-window parable remains the cleanest illustration of opportunity cost ever written.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on development economics.
recommendations.reason: The episode Amit calls 'profoundly important', tying growth to welfare and pushing back on redistribution-first framings.

recommendations.item: Economic Growth Is Enough and Only Economic Growth Is Enough
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Pritchett's paper on growth and human welfare indicators.
recommendations.reason: Pritchett's empirical claim: across a wide gamut of human welfare indicators, around 99% of variation correlates with per-capita GDP. The remaining 1% is where redistribution and welfarism live.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on the state.
recommendations.reason: The starting-point for the argument that whatever the government does is paid for by taxes, and that those taxes are coercive.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Episode 55)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on Indian infrastructure.
recommendations.reason: The episode that dismantles the modern Indian assumption that every new road and airport is an unalloyed good — diminishing returns and roads-to-nowhere are real.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression
recommendations.creator: Amity Shlaes
recommendations.context: Shlaes' revisionist account of the Great Depression.
recommendations.reason: A counterpoint to the standard narrative that Roosevelt's New Deal stimulus rescued America — referenced as the alternative reading on Depression-era public works.

recommendations.item: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on innovation policy.
recommendations.reason: Where Amit and Ajay argue against state-funded prestige projects (the Indian space program among them) on the grounds of opportunity cost.

recommendations.item: Who Lends to the Indian State?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and co-authors
recommendations.context: An XKDR Forum paper measuring India's financial repression.
recommendations.reason: The first paper to put a number on it — the headline summary is that 95% of the borrowing of the Indian state is coerced out of the financial system. A direct measurement of the Hazlitt-style problem of governments crowding out private credit.

recommendations.item: The Globalisation Episode (Episode 95)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on globalisation.
recommendations.reason: Where the case against tariffs is made in detail — they redistribute wealth from poor consumers to rich producers.

recommendations.item: Is Globalization Doomed? (Episode 96)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE follow-up on globalisation.
recommendations.reason: Companion to Episode 95 on whether the global trading order can survive the current wave of protectionism.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on price controls.
recommendations.reason: Amit's own crisp summary of why every price control ultimately hurts the very people it claims to protect.

recommendations.item: Prices, Fast and Slow
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's NIPFP paper on prices.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's own paper extending the Hayekian view of prices as society's information system.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Episode 67)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on exchange rates.
recommendations.reason: The argument that exchange rates are prices too, and rigging them produces the same shortages and distortions as any other price control.

recommendations.item: Episode 14 of The Seen and the Unseen on Rent Control
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: An early, twenty-minute, Bastiat-inspired Seen and Unseen episode.
recommendations.reason: A concise primer on why rent control destroys housing supply — the only Seen and Unseen rent-control episode, and a model of the show in its earliest form.

recommendations.item: The Mystery of Capital
recommendations.creator: Hernando de Soto
recommendations.context: De Soto's masterpiece on property rights and dead capital.
recommendations.reason: Source of the indispensable 'dead capital' concept — without property rights, slum dwellers and tribals cannot leverage the houses and land they effectively own. Amit argues rent control similarly converts apartments into dead capital.

recommendations.item: Daniel Hannan's Tweet on the Left and Compassion
recommendations.creator: Daniel Hannan
recommendations.context: A tweet that landed on the day of recording.
recommendations.reason: Hannan's framing: the defining characteristic of the left is not compassion but the conviction that compassion is unique to its side, leading to a grotesque misunderstanding of what the other side thinks.

recommendations.item: Milton Friedman on the Minimum Wage
recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: A short Friedman video clip on YouTube.
recommendations.reason: Friedman's classic walk-through of why the minimum wage hurts the very workers it purports to help — a video Amit recommends for readers who want a quick, lucid version of Hazlitt's chapter on minimum wage.

recommendations.item: India Awakes
recommendations.creator: Johan Norberg (presenter); Free to Choose Foundation (producer)
recommendations.context: A documentary on Indian markets and freedom.
recommendations.reason: Contains the Barun Mitra story of using historical Google Earth satellite imagery to establish tribal land tenure in Gujarat — and what changed (pakka houses, toilets) the moment the tribals had property rights.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen Episode on Demonetisation with Suyash Rai
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
recommendations.context: An early Seen and Unseen episode on demonetisation.
recommendations.reason: Source of the moral argument that cost-benefit analyses are intrinsically immoral when the cost falls on one group and the benefit on another; by contrast, demonetisation produced no real benefits and was a disaster for the poor.

core_ideas.concept: The Seen and the Unseen (Hazlitt's One Lesson)
core_ideas.explanation: The bad economist sees only the immediate effect on one visible group. The good economist looks at the longer-run effects and the effects on all groups. The whole book is one extended application of this single discipline. The shopkeeper's broken window appears to stimulate the economy because we see the glazier earn his fee, but we don't see the suit the shopkeeper would otherwise have bought; the tailor's lost commission is the unseen.
core_ideas.quote: The bad economist sees only what immediately strikes the eye. The good economist also looks beyond. The bad economist sees only what the effect of a given policy has or will be on one particular group. The good economist inquires also what the effect of the policy will be on all groups.

core_ideas.explanation: Manufacturing an EV by assembling a lithium-ion battery in Igatpuri and manufacturing it by exporting frozen chicken from JNPT in exchange for a foreign-built EV are two ways of solving the same problem. Both are technologies. Tariffs that protect the Igatpuri-EV are an industrial policy choosing one technology over another — exactly the kind of state winner-picking the show has long argued against. To shut down trade is to shut down a technology, and committing to autarky is the trade equivalent of becoming a Luddite.
core_ideas.quote: What is happening at JNPT is a piece of magic that converts frozen chicken into electric vehicles.

core_ideas.explanation: Our default intuitions are zero-sum and top-down because that's how we're wired. But certain ideas — the price system, spontaneous order, opportunity cost — produce 'light bulb' moments after which the old intuition is replaced. The point of books like Hazlitt's, and shows like EIE, is to deliver light bulbs. Once on, they cannot be switched off; the new view of the world becomes the new default intuition.
core_ideas.quote: We are constantly throwing light bulbs at the screen — not literally throwing light bulbs at the screen, which would be throwing light bulbs at the camera.

core_ideas.explanation: Every public job created by a bridge project destroys a private job somewhere else: the 10 million dollars taken from taxpayers to build it would have employed automobile workers, television technicians, clothing workers and farmers. We can see the bridge-builders. We cannot see what the unbuilt private economy would have looked like. The corollary is that 'projects have to be invented' — instead of asking where bridges must be built, governments start asking where bridges can be built, dressing political optics as infrastructure.
core_ideas.quote: For every public job created by the bridge project, a private job has been destroyed somewhere else.

core_ideas.explanation: Equating taxes with time turns the abstraction concrete: if a third of your income goes to the government, you work four months of the year for the state and not yourself. Half your income, six months. With the GST and other indirect taxes layered on top, real total taxation is far higher than most people realise — even the beggar at the traffic signal pays tax when she buys soap. This isn't an argument against all taxes (rights protection requires some), but a discipline for taking them seriously.

Finance is information-processing, forecasting and risk-taking. Bureaucracies have no incentive to do this complex work, no tolerance for the failure that finance requires (some loans must go bad), and they are pulled into political capture: priority-sector lending, grabbing money for the state through financial repression, or rescuing favoured borrowers. XKDR's measurement: 95% of the Indian state's borrowing is coerced out of the financial system. Successful countries keep the government out of finance.
core_ideas.quote: Why do you rob banks? Because that's where the money is.

core_ideas.concept: The Curse of Machinery (and Why It Was Always Wrong)
core_ideas.explanation: Every generation re-runs the same complaint: this technology will destroy jobs. Adam Smith showed pin-makers' productivity going from 1 to 4,800 pins a day; if labour-displacement were the whole story, the industry would have had 99.98% unemployment. Instead, productivity gains went out into the economy as cheaper goods, freed-up labour, new industries and rising real wages. Today's Luddites apply the argument to AI. The historical sample size is large enough by now: there is no reason to think it is different this time. If you really believe machines destroy jobs, you should be pushing rail freight back onto people's backs.
core_ideas.quote: The aggregate consumption of society is the aggregate production of society.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's clean reframing: a society can only consume what it produces, so productivity gains are by definition gains in per-capita consumption. There is no better cause than productivity growth, and the technology debate should always come back to this identity. Adoption of new technology takes time (steam engines, electricity, spreadsheets), which gives society space to retrain and adjust; the doomster fantasy of an overnight transformation is rarely how history actually moves.

core_ideas.concept: Culture Determines Whether Technology Heals or Divides
core_ideas.explanation: Every technological transformation hurts some workers, firms, creditors and dealerships. A society dominated by class-warfare narratives turns these wrenching adjustments into nuclear-reactor explosions: anti-elitism, populism, and the next Donald Trump. A society of harmony — Ajay's 'more Gandhi-ji and less Karl Marx' — treats them as ordinary life events that we deal with collaboratively. Marx's claim that history is the history of class warfare wasn't a description of reality so much as an instruction for how to make it real.
core_ideas.quote: When Karl Marx said that the history of the world is a history of class warfare, it's not a fair description of the world as it is. It is a fair description of the world as he sought to make it.

core_ideas.explanation: The state's instinct to 'save' a struggling indigenous industry — jute in West Bengal, automobiles via tariffs, anything 'ours' — always carries hidden costs: subsidies must be funded, price controls distort signals, special treatment crowds out other industries that don't get the favour. Hazlitt's chapter title is the trick: anything called 'saving' an industry is in fact transferring resources to it from somewhere unseen. Postscript: jute did just fine without state coddling, riding technological forces all by itself.

Rent control rewires every incentive in housing. Landlords stop maintaining the building (Marine Drive's dilapidated flats with rents of a few hundred rupees a month). Developers stop building rental stock. Tenants over-occupy because they don't economise on space. New entrants can't find housing — Bombay went from 1942's fifteen-minute rentals to a market in which renting felt impossible. De Soto's 'dead capital' concept applies: the apartment is no longer leverageable for the owner and not owned by the tenant either; it serves nobody. Rent control is a slow-motion theft, and Mamdani's New York campaign shows the lesson hasn't been learned.
core_ideas.quote: The greatest fertilizer of all is the tender gaze of an owner. — James C. Scott

core_ideas.explanation: Daniel Hannan's tweet captures it: many on the left believe compassion is the proprietary preserve of their side, which produces a grotesque misunderstanding of the other. The truly compassionate person is the one who looks past intentions and asks: do these policies actually help those they claim to help? Rent control, minimum wage and price controls all flunk that test. Virtue-signalling on Twitter about lower rents is what passes as caring; thinking through second-order effects is what caring actually is.
core_ideas.quote: The defining characteristic of the left is not compassion. Rather, it is a conviction that compassion is unique to their side.

core_ideas.explanation: A lot of bad policy survives because its boosters frame it virtuously. 'Increase credit' = 'increase debt'. 'Increase farm prices' = 'make food dearer for the city worker'. 'Increase exports' = 'increase imports'. 'Government subsidies' = 'increased taxes'. 'Increase wage rates' (legislatively) = 'increase production costs'. The discipline of restating any economic claim from the opposite side reveals what is really being said and shifts the moral weight of the argument.
core_ideas.quote: When they say that the way to economic salvation is to increase credit, it is just as if they said that the way to economic salvation is to increase debt.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Talk About 'Society' — Talk About People
core_ideas.explanation: Many fallacies hide inside abstractions like 'the nation', 'the collective' or 'society'. Margaret Thatcher's correction stands: there are individuals; the smallest minority is the individual. When someone speaks about 'the good of society', the discipline is to stop and ask which actual people are helped, which actual people are harmed, and to evaluate the policy on those terms.
core_ideas.quote: There are men regarded today as brilliant economists who deprecate saving and recommend squandering on a national scale as a way of economic salvation.

core_ideas.explanation: In our personal lives we are all libertarian — when four friends order food, no one forces another to eat or pay; we don't steal from a stranger to fund our own meal; we don't dream of telling close friends how to live. But abstract one level out, to the state and 'society', and we suddenly accept coercion, social engineering, even imprisonment for unpaid taxes. Adam Smith's old line: what is prudence in the private family can scarcely be folly in a great nation. The discipline is to reconcile our personal ethics with what we tolerate from the state.
core_ideas.quote: What is prudence in the conduct of every private family can scarce be folly in that of a great kingdom. — Adam Smith

core_ideas.concept: Cost-Benefit Has a Hidden Morality Problem
core_ideas.explanation: Suyash Rai's point on demonetisation: when policy analysts do cost-benefit calculations, they often forget that the cost is borne by one group of people and the benefit by another. There is an inherent immorality to that asymmetry — particularly when, as with demonetisation, the costs were on the poor and the supposed benefits were imagined and deferred. Aggregate numbers wash out the distributional injustice; the discipline is to refuse the wash and ask whose lives are paying for whose abstraction.
core_ideas.quote: In the long run, we are all dead.

core_ideas.explanation: Five frameworks for evaluating any policy. (1) Opportunity cost — for every seen effect, ask what is the unseen alternative. (2) General welfare, not interest-group welfare — look beyond the protected group to the whole economy. (3) Incentives and distortions — taxes change behaviour; price controls distort the system. (4) The price system as miraculous information — prices are how dispersed knowledge gets aggregated; treat them as sacred. (5) Capital formation — savings, investment and the long-run productive base of the economy.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on Amit's secret project: 'The FSB scrape YouTube. They will hear the words secret project and now they will start tapping your phone.' Amit: 'What is the FSB?' Ajay: 'The FSB is the new name of the KGB.'
Amit, on Ajay puking on a forest from a paraglider: 'If you puke on a forest but nobody sees it, did you puke?'

Amit on Hazlitt updating the book: 'In 1961 he added one chapter on rent control. But he didn't change a word in the rest of the book... it's a similar thing to physics. After Newton, Einstein comes along much later. But broadly, once you know the basic principles, they hold.'
Amit's running joke about Hazlitt's archetypes: 'Bad economists and good economists, or Bengali economists and non-Bengali, or Gujarati and non-Gujarati economists, but we shall leave that aside.'

Ajay's vision for show merch: 'There will be a cannon placed near the TV that shoots out used defunct tungsten bulbs, programmed so that from inside the show Amit gets to control when the light bulb gets shot at the user.' Amit: 'Why use tungsten bulbs? We will spend the best bulbs.'

Ajay's cheeky post-script about the Indian space program: an Indian astronaut was put into space using a foreign launch provider. 'Carry this to the logical conclusion — really what you need is AI. Just visual effects of an astronaut being put into space or a lander walking on the moon. You get the full propaganda value at very low cost.'

Amit, on the moon-conspiracy detour: 'This reminds me of the conspiracy theory that the moon landings happened in Nevada — which of course they did not, they happened on the moon. We are fairly certain of that.'
Ajay on the standard line about the Great Recession: 'In the long run, the economy would have clawed back. Most of the time, yeah, I would agree we should not be exuberant about infrastructure.'

Amit, on a Bengali bureaucrat doing classic make-work: stares him down, then narrates the failed exchange where the bureaucrat gave up after forty-five milliseconds. Ajay: 'Forty-five milliseconds later.'

Amit on his own Bengali identity: 'In case you wonder why we make so many jokes about Bengalis, dear readers, it's because I am a Bengali. The name doesn't indicate it, but I am a Bengali, and he doesn't like Bengali economists in particular, and I don't like being holier-than-thou economists either.'
Ajay's t-shirt slogan for EIE merch: 'Make trade not war.' Amit: 'So do you prefer making trade or making — Unprintable, is it?'

Ajay defending Mamdani's age: 'He who is not a communist when he is young has no heart. He who is a communist as an adult has no brain. So give him a break. Maybe he's got to figure out his economics.' Amit: 'Thirty-four is old enough.'

Amit, after Ajay calls his mentee 'a mini Ajay': 'How do you think of the idea of young Ajays, male and female, running around the world, talking like you, thinking like you?' Ajay: 'They'll soon get over the delusion that there is anything here which is somehow special.' Amit: 'Oh my god, such modesty, Ajay.'
George Santayana, The Life of Reason (1905): 'Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.' — invoked against the recurring Luddite panic about new technology.
Margaret Thatcher's 'Don't speak to me of society. There are individuals.' — invoked as the discipline against fuzzy talk of 'the good of society'.
Arthur C. Clarke's third law: 'Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.' — re-applied to JNPT, where frozen chicken arrives as electric vehicles.
James C. Scott, Seeing Like a State: 'The greatest fertilizer of all is the tender gaze of an owner.' — Ajay's chosen line on why property rights matter for land improvement.

Adam Smith's pin factory, from Chapter 1 of The Wealth of Nations: a workman without machinery could scarcely make one pin a day; with machinery, 4,800. Hazlitt deploys it against every Luddite generation.
Frederic Bastiat's 'Parable of the Broken Window' — the boy who breaks a shopkeeper's window does not stimulate the economy; he merely diverts it from the unseen tailor's commission.
John Maynard Keynes' 'In the long run we are all dead' — Hazlitt's swipe at flippant short-termism, and Amit's later (sympathetic) re-deployment against deferred-benefit cost-benefit analysis.

Zohran Mamdani — winner of the New York Democratic primary for mayor, son of filmmaker Mira Nair and academic Mahmood Mamdani; Amit calls him charming but his economic policies (rent control, government grocery stores, free buses) the worst excesses of the 20th century.
Gunnar Myrdal — Nobel-winning economist who claimed automation was good for the West but bad for India because labour demand would fall; held up here as 'a Nobel Prize for talking nonsense.'
The American bank-robber line attributed to Willie Sutton: 'Why do you rob banks? Because that's where the money is.' — applied to policymakers raiding the financial system.
